title: The Ultimate Qantas Economy Class Seat Guide
body:
Australian Frequent Flyer
Australian Frequent Flyer - Tips, Tricks and Chat for Australian Frequent Flyers
Qantas A380 Economy Class seats. Photo: Qantas.
Subtly, every aircraft is different. If you’re flying in Economy on a Qantas Airbus A380, for example, your seat won’t be the same as on a Boeing 787 or 737.
So, what are the differences between the Economy Class seats on different Qantas planes? Which aircraft has the most comfortable seats? And which are the best and worst seats on each Qantas aircraft type ?
This guide explains what you need to know about all the different Qantas Economy Class seats, in order from best to worst.
Qantas Airbus A380 Economy Class
Economy Class on the Qantas A380 is laid out in a standard 3-4-3 configuration on the lower deck. There used to also be a small Economy cabin at the rear of the upper deck, but this was removed during the A380 cabin refurbishments .
Qantas A380 Economy cabin. Photo: Qantas.
The Qantas A380 seats are perfectly comfortable, as far as Economy seats go. There are TV screens on the back of each seat, but no Wi-Fi is available.
If you want some extra legroom, the exit row seats are a good choice – although Qantas charges extra for these. For solo travellers, the best Qantas A380 Economy seats are 71D, 80A and 80K because there is no seat in front. (The space where seat 70D should be is an emergency exit for the crew rest compartment.)
If you’re thinking about lying down across a row of empty seats, beware that the armrests on the Qantas A380 do not lift up fully (only a little). If you’re in a bulkhead row, the armrest is fixed as there is a tray table inside it, and legroom can be restricted due to the position of the wall. (This is also the case in the bulkhead rows on most other aircraft types.)
Key facts: Qantas A380 Economy seats
Seat pitch: 31 inches
Seat width: 18 inches
In-flight entertainment: In-seat Panasonic entertainment screens
Best seats: 71D, 80A, 80K & other exit row seats
Qantas Airbus A330 Economy Class
There are several different versions of the Qantas Airbus A330. On each one, Economy Class is in a comfortable 2-4-2 configuration.
Qantas A330-300 Economy seats. Photo: Matt Graham.
There are some small differences between each type, but in general the best seats are the Economy Plus and exit row seats. These seats offer extra legroom and can be selected for a fee, or for free if you have Qantas Platinum or Platinum One status. (Qantas is currently in the process of rolling out Economy Plus on its A330 fleet, and it’s not yet available on all aircraft.)
The exit door blocks some of the legroom of the exit row window seats, but this is not a huge inconvenience.
The bulkhead seats in rows 23 and 24 (on most configurations) are also good for daytime flights, but there is a wall in front of the seats which prevents you from fully stretching your legs out.
Most Qantas A330-200s and some A330-300s have free Wi-Fi available (it will eventually be installed across the whole fleet). This now also works when flying outside of Australian airspace.
Qantas A330-300 Economy Class
On the Qantas Airbus A330-300, all seats have seat-back entertainment screens and a net for your feet . This is the best of the Qantas A330 Economy products. Note that seats 28A and 28K have a missing window.
Qantas Airbus A330-300 Economy Class. Photo: Matt Graham.
Qantas A330-200 Economy Class (international long-haul version)
The Qantas A330-200 Economy seats on the international version are almost the same as on the A330-300, albeit a different colour. There are seatback TV screens for each seat, but no foot nets.
This version of the A330-200 has slightly fewer seats than the other one. It’s mainly used on routes like Brisbane-Los Angeles, Sydney-Bengaluru, Melbourne-Delhi and Melbourne-Jakarta.
The seat pairs by the windows between rows 24 and 33 have extra legroom and are designated as Economy Plus seats.
Qantas A330-200 Economy Class (domestic/short-haul version)
The Economy seats on the domestic version of the Qantas A330-200 have the same basic design as the international version but there are no seat-back TV screens. Instead, Qantas provides iPads in the seat pockets with entertainment content that you can stream. Beware that row 26 on this aircraft has no window.
The seat pairs by the windows between rows 24 and 36 are Economy Plus seats with more legroom.
This aircraft is mainly used on domestic and trans-Tasman routes, as well as some flights to Denpasar, Singapore, Manila and Jakarta.
Qantas A330-200 domestic Economy cabin. Photo: Matt Graham.
Ex-Finnair A330-300s
If you’re flying on one of the ex-Finnair A330-300s that have Premium Economy seating, you’ll get a different type of seat. The good news is that Finnair’s A330 Economy Class is comfortable .
On this aircraft, the seats in the centre section (D, E, G and H) between rows 31 and 36 are Economy Plus and have more legroom.
Finnair A330-300 Economy Class seats. Photo: Matt Graham.
Key facts: Qantas A330 Economy seats
Seat pitch: 31 inches (or 34 inches in Economy Plus)
Seat width: 18 inches
In-flight entertainment: In-seat Panasonic entertainment screens, except on the short-haul A330-200 which has iPads
Best seats: Exit row and Economy Plus seats, which vary by configuration
Seats to avoid: 28A & 28K (window missing on A330-300)
Qantas Airbus A321XLR Economy Class
The Airbus A321XLR is the newest plane type in the Qantas fleet. At the moment, it’s mainly used on domestic routes.
These seats are wider than the Boeing 737 and 787 Economy seats, and the legroom is alright. As an added bonus, the overhead lockers on these jets are particularly large.
These seats include USB-A and USB-C charging outlets, a flip-down device holder for a tablet or phone, and there’s free Wi-Fi for everyone on board. However, there are no seat-back TV screens.
Qantas Airbus A321XLR Economy Class. Photo: Qantas.
There are six rows of Economy Plus seats with extra legroom on the Qantas A321XLR. The pick of the bunch would be row 6, which is the front row of Economy and directly behind the Business Class partition. The exit rows 15 and 16 have more legroom as well, as do rows 7, 17 and 18.
Key facts: Qantas A321XLR Economy seats
Seat pitch: 30 inches
Seat width: 18 inches
In-flight entertainment: Streaming entertainment to your own device + free high-speed Wi-Fi
Best seats: Rows 6, 7, 15, 16, 17 & 18
Seats to avoid: Row 35 (the last row) is close to the toilets, which often have queues.
Qantas Boeing 787-9 Economy Class
The Economy seats on Qantas’ Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner are ergonomically designed with good padding. They have a great in-flight entertainment system and also have the most legroom of any Qantas aircraft. But with a 3-3-3 layout, these seats are too narrow for comfort on long flights such as London-Perth . We’d suggest choosing a different aircraft type if possible.
Qantas Boeing 787-9 Economy Class. Photo: Qantas.
If you are booked to fly on a Qantas Dreamliner in Economy, you may consider trying to get an upgrade. Failing that, the up-front bulkhead seats in rows 40 and 46 have a bit of extra legroom.
Otherwise, there aren’t really any standout seats. If you’re travelling as a couple, there are two seat pairs by the windows in row 59. If possible, avoid sitting near the toilets because you’ll be able to hear them flushing during the whole flight.
There is a TV screen at every seat, but no Wi-Fi.
Key facts: Qantas 787 Economy seats
Seat pitch: 32 inches
Seat width: 17 inches
In-flight entertainment: In-seat Panasonic entertainment screens (newest generation)
Best seats: Rows 40 or 46
Seats to avoid: Rows 44 and 57 do not have a window, and avoid sitting near the toilets.
Qantas Boeing 737-800 Economy Class
Qantas 737 Economy Class. Photo: Qantas.
Qantas’ Boeing 737-800s offer the least comfortable Economy Class experience of the Qantas mainline fleet. But these narrow-body aircraft are mostly used for domestic flights and shorter international routes. Alt …
